conventions: Each unit is a word of the vocabulary: a repeatable action with an entry state, phases, key shapes and an exit state. Durations are expressions the grammar evaluates with the unit's parameters and the physics of the envelope (grammar.PHYSICS); shapes combine the pose library's regions (poses.json) at fractions of a phase. Sides: S supports, G gestures; the grammar mirrors a unit by swapping them. Support states: both, S, G, none (in the air), floor (hands, knees or seat). Momentum classes: still (under 0.15 m/s), travelling, turning. Effort follows Laban's four factors. 'lunar' says what the Moon's gravity and air change, with figures from the envelope product; 'native' units exist only at partial gravity in air.
evidence: Units drawn from ballet, modern and contemporary dance, ballroom, Mevlevi turning, Chinese classical water-sleeve technique, contact improvisation and acrobatics (sources.json), and lunar units designed from the envelope's mechanics. Durations and limits are physics screens; the motion engine tests each realised unit with whole-body dynamics.

families.level: Rise, fall, balance and leg gestures
families.flight: Elevation: jumps and what happens aloft
families.floor: Level changes to and from the floor

units.name: glide step
units.description: A step that rolls heel to toe and transfers the weight forward while the free leg brushes past the standing foot; the body travels level, with no bob.
units.lunar: adapted: the step period stretches toward the leg's lunar pendulum (about 1.0-1.4 s) and the body cannot bob, since the centre of mass never drops faster than g; speed changes by at most 0.8 m/s^2 against the floor's grip.
units.garment: skirt sways with the step; sleeves trail at walking speed (air outweighs a chiffon sleeve 19 to 1 at 1 m/s)
checks: centre of pressure inside the foot

units.name: balancé (rise and fall)
units.description: Down-up-up in three beats: a step into a soft knee, two steps on the balls of the feet, then the fall back down.
units.lunar: adapted: the rise is muscle-quick, the fall is gravity-slow; at 1/6 g a 6 cm descent takes at least 0.38 s (Earth 0.16 s), so the lunar balancé lingers at the top of its rise and settles like a breath.
units.garment: skirt lifts on the fall and lands after the feet

units.name: orbit run
units.source: lunar, from ballroom's curved progression and the Apollo lope
units.description: Low bounding strides around a circle, each a short flight, the body leaning into the centre; speed builds or bleeds stride by stride.
units.lunar: native: a level turn at speed v needs radius v^2/(mu g): 4.9 m at 2 m/s on the Moon against 0.8 m on Earth, so travel at speed curves in wide orbits; each stance can add or take up to mu N T / m of speed, so building 2 m/s takes 2.5 m of floor. Leaning into the circle by atan(v^2/(g r)) gives deep, visible inclines (17 deg at 1 m/s on a 2 m circle, where Earth leans 3 deg). A bounding stride presses the floor hard enough to change the speed by about 0.8 m/s, three times a walking step's 0.27, which is why lunar travel bounds.
units.garment: the skirt streams outward and back; sleeves stream behind nearly horizontal

units.name: tombé (falling step)
units.description: From a raised leg the dancer falls onto it, the knee taking the weight into a lunge.
units.lunar: adapted: the fall is the point and the Moon slows it 2.45 times; a tombé can be a long lean taken in a single held breath.
units.garment: the skirt trails the fall and swings past the lunge

units.name: pas de bourrée
units.description: Three quick changes of weight, back-side-front, that change the supporting foot and redirect travel.
units.lunar: adapted: quick footwork keeps Earth's muscle tempo, so the three changes can stay quick while the body above barely moves; each step can shift the travel by at most 0.8 m/s^2 times its stance.
units.garment: the skirt hardly responds

units.name: plié and relevé
units.description: A bend of the knees over the toes and a rise through the feet onto demi-pointe.
units.lunar: adapted: down is gravity-clocked, up is muscle-clocked. A grand plié of 0.35 m cannot descend and stop in less than 0.93 s (0.38 s on Earth), yet the rise can come back in a third of that: the lunar plié sinks and springs.
units.garment: the skirt pools a little on the descent and lifts on the rise

units.name: développé
units.description: The gesture leg draws up through passé and unfolds to its height.
units.lunar: adapted: holding a leg at 90 deg asks a sixth of Earth's hip torque against gravity (the leg's inertia is unchanged), so extensions can rise higher, hold far longer and unfold more slowly.
units.garment: the skirt rides up the lifted leg and falls slowly back

units.name: long penché
units.description: From arabesque the trunk tips forward and down while the leg rises behind, the body rotating about the supporting hip like a slow see-saw; it can pass the point where an Earth dancer would have to step.
units.lunar: native: the inverted-pendulum time constant is 0.75 s (Earth 0.30 s), so the dancer can hang at the edge of balance and correct with a sixth of the ankle torque; the line is held for seconds.
units.garment: the skirt hangs from the hips and slides along the raised leg

units.name: long fall
units.source: lunar, from Humphrey's fall and recovery
units.description: A deliberate fall from balance: the dancer gives the body to gravity, tipping as one piece, and catches it at the last moment in a lunge, a step or onto the hands.
units.lunar: native: from 2 deg off vertical to 45 deg takes 2.9 s on the Moon (1.2 s on Earth); the dancer can turn the head, open the arms or begin a spiral inside the fall and still catch it.
units.garment: the sleeves stay above as the body tips under them

units.name: fall and recovery
units.description: A swing of the whole body away from balance and its rebound back through the vertical, with a suspension at the top.
units.lunar: adapted: suspension at the top of the rebound stretches with the slower pendulum; the arc reads as breath.
units.garment: the skirt swings in the fall's direction and returns after the body

units.name: pirouette
units.description: A turn on one foot, the other in passé, arms gathered, the head spotting.
units.lunar: adapted: the floor's grip gives the turn 8.9 N m of torque against Earth's 54, so a two-revolution-per-second turn needs about 0.8 s of preparation; once turning, pivot friction stops it only after about 10 revolutions (Earth under 2). The lunar pirouette starts slowly and keeps going.
units.garment: a skirt with weight flares in the turn; light chiffon winds around the body (garment solver)

units.name: whirl
units.description: A sustained turn travelling slowly on a circle, the left foot pivoting while the right gives small pushes; arms open, the skirt standing out.
units.lunar: native in degree: pivot friction spends a sixth of the spin, so a slow whirl of 0.3-0.5 revolutions a second continues with the lightest pushes. Without air a skirt would flare to 45-60 deg at these rates (Earth needs 45-55 rpm); in the Moon's dense air the air winds a light skirt around the body instead (chiffon opens 10-13 deg at 5-20 rpm in the garment solver), so the whirling skirt needs weight.
units.garment: the skirt's flare is the figure when the skirt has weight (satin opens 16-23 deg at 15-20 rpm); sleeves spiral out

units.name: spiral descent
units.source: contemporary (spiral to the floor), ballroom contra-body
units.description: A turn that winds the body down to a kneel or the floor, the torso leading the hips.
units.lunar: adapted: the descent cannot outpace g, so the spiral sinks slowly through more turning than on Earth.
units.garment: the skirt wraps and then opens across the floor

units.name: sauté (suspended)
units.description: A jump from two feet to two feet with the legs straight and pointed in the air.
units.lunar: adapted: Earth's petit allegro tempo (a jump every half second) would rise 5 cm here; the lunar sauté is a slow hang: a 0.6 m rise floats 1.7 s.
units.garment: the skirt rises late and blooms upward on the descent

units.name: skim
units.source: lunar, from ballet's bourrée and the Apollo crews' hop
units.description: A run of tiny hops a few centimetres high, quick underneath and level above, so the dancer seems to travel on air just above the floor.
units.lunar: native: a 0.5 m/s push rises 7.7 cm and lasts 0.62 s (Earth 0.10 s); a stream of such hops keeps the body level while the feet patter, a gliding travel without sliding.
units.garment: the skirt hovers almost still while the feet move

units.name: grand jeté (suspended)
units.description: A travelling leap from one foot to the other with the legs thrown into a split.
units.lunar: adapted: at half the dancer's maximal rise (1.4 m) the leap lasts 2.7 s against 0.5 s on Earth, so the split becomes a held line where on Earth it is a flash at the apex; travel at 1.5 m/s carries it 4.0 m and the stage needs 6.8 m with approach and run-out.
units.garment: the skirt opens with the split and blooms on the descent

units.name: flight phrase
units.source: lunar, from ballet's jeté passé and contemporary aerial shapes
units.description: One long flight that carries a sequence of shapes: open, gather, open the other way, each held long enough to read, before the landing.
units.lunar: native: a 2.7-3.3 s flight holds three or four shapes of 0.7-0.8 s each, where Earth's 0.5 s holds one; the flight becomes a sentence.
units.garment: each shape change sends a wave through skirt and sleeves that arrives after the shape
checks: zero angular momentum or a planned reorientation

units.name: slow salto
units.description: A whole somersault in a long, open layout line, turning as slowly as a wheel, landed on the feet.
units.lunar: native: one layout somersault over a 2.7 s flight needs 22 N m s of angular momentum, a fifth of Earth's 121 for its maximal 0.5 s flight; the rotation is slow enough to read as a shape turning.
units.garment: the skirt inverts with the body and lags, opening like a bell as the feet come over

units.name: unfolding turn
units.source: lunar, from ballet's tour en l'air
units.description: A jump that leaves the floor turning slowly, gathers to spin faster, then opens to slow again before landing: an accelerando and ritardando inside one flight.
units.lunar: native: with angular momentum fixed in flight, gathering the arms from second to first speeds the twist 2.6 times (inertia 1.51 to 0.58 kg m^2); over a 2.7 s flight the change in tempo is visible, where on Earth the whole jump is over in 0.5 s.
units.garment: the skirt flares and narrows with the spin's tempo

units.name: carve
units.source: lunar, from skiing's carved turn and ballroom's curved steps
units.description: A landing that changes direction: the dancer lands on a bent leg leaning into the new path and lets the floor's push bend the travel.
units.lunar: native: a 2.5 m/s landing absorbed over 0.4 m loads the floor 5.8 lunar body weights and can turn 1.5 m/s of travel; since grip on level running is so weak, landings are where a lunar dancer steers.
units.garment: the skirt swings wide around the new curve
checks: turn within mu N T / m

units.name: kneel and rise
units.description: Lowering to one knee and rising again through the standing leg.
units.lunar: adapted: lowering is slow (gravity) and rising takes a sixth of the work; floor work becomes a matter of descending well.
units.garment: the skirt pools around the knee and lifts after the rise

units.name: rise from the floor
units.description: From kneeling or sitting, the dancer gathers the feet under the hips and rises through one leg to standing.
units.lunar: adapted: rising lifts a sixth of Earth's weight, so it can be quick and nearly effortless; it is the way down that takes time.
units.garment: the skirt is drawn up off the floor and falls slowly after the rise

units.name: port de bras
units.description: The arms carried through positions with the torso, head and gaze following.
units.lunar: adapted: the arms weigh a sixth, so they float and can be held and carried for long phrases; their inertia keeps Earth's, so a quick arm still asks Earth's effort and still pushes the body.
units.garment: sleeves follow with a lag of a second or more

units.name: contraction and release
units.description: The pelvis and spine curl in from the centre and open out again.
units.lunar: adapted: unchanged in its muscular core; at 1/6 g a strong contraction can lift the dancer off the floor if done on a jump, joining floor and air.
units.garment: the skirt jumps with the pelvis

units.name: sleeve cast
units.source: Chinese classical water-sleeve dance (throwing, 抛袖)
units.description: A whip of the arm from the shoulder to the wrist that throws the sleeve out to its full length.
units.lunar: adapted: a chiffon sleeve thrown upward settles at 0.23 m/s face-on (Earth 0.60), staying aloft 6.6 s for each 1.5 m of fall; the cast's line hangs in the air long after the arm has moved on.
units.garment: the sleeve's flight is the figure

units.name: canopy
units.source: lunar, from water-sleeve throwing and veil dance
units.description: Both sleeves are cast high so that they open overhead and settle slowly over the dancer, who moves beneath them and gathers them as they arrive.
units.lunar: native: chiffon falling face-on at 0.23 m/s gives 6-8 s under a descending canopy; on Earth it is down in 2.5 s, and in microgravity it never comes down.
units.garment: the canopy is the figure; recovery gathers it before the next step
checks: sleeves clear of the face and feet

units.name: sleeve gather
units.source: Chinese classical water-sleeve dance (recovering, 收袖)
units.description: Rolling the wrist and drawing the arm in so that the free sleeve winds back onto the forearm.
units.lunar: adapted: the gather takes as long as the sleeve takes to come within reach, which the air decides; the dancer waits on the fabric, a new kind of rest.
units.garment: the sleeve winds onto the forearm

units.name: one-arm lift
units.source: ballet pas de deux, contact improvisation
units.description: One dancer raises the other overhead on a single arm and walks with them.
units.lunar: native: the partner weighs 89 N, within a strong one-arm press; the lifted dancer's inertia is Earth's, so starting and stopping the walk still takes the floor's grip.
units.garment: the lifted dancer's skirt hangs and swings slowly

units.name: toss and catch
units.description: One dancer throws the other upward to turn or open in the air and catches them on the descent.
units.lunar: native: a two-arm push of 350 N over 0.6 m launches a 55 kg partner 1.75 m up for 2.9 s; on Earth the same push cannot lift them.
units.garment: the thrown dancer's skirt and sleeves bloom above the catch
